section.title: A Song of Trust
section.sectionRationale: This song of Judah continues the Isaiah apocalypse, chapters 24 to 27, turning from the LORD's cosmic judgment and banquet of chapter 25 to a sustained hymn about trusting Him as the Rock eternal. It reaches one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of bodily resurrection, your dead will live, their bodies will rise, before calling God's people to hide briefly until His wrath has passed.
section.thesis: The LORD keeps in perfect peace all who trust in Him as the Rock eternal, and though His people may labor in distress and seem to accomplish nothing lasting, He promises that their dead will live and their bodies will rise, so they can safely hide until His wrath against the earth has passed.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the strong city whose walls are salvation, and trust in the eternal Rock; the level path of the righteous who wait for the LORD's judgments; peace established and other lords renounced; labor pains that produced nothing lasting; and the resurrection promise followed by a call to hide until the wrath passes.

units.label: A strong city, trust in the eternal Rock

verses.text: In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: We have a strong city; salvation is established as its walls and ramparts.
Open the gates so a righteous nation may enter, one that remains faithful.
You will keep in perfect {{shalom|peace}} the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You.
Trust in the LORD forever, because GOD the LORD is the {{tsurOlamim|Rock eternal}}.
For He has humbled those who dwell on high; He lays the lofty city low. He brings it down to the ground; He casts it into the dust.
Feet trample it down, the feet of the oppressed, the steps of the poor.

units.label: The level path of the righteous

verses.text: The path of the righteous is level; You clear a straight path for the upright.
Yes, we wait for You, O LORD; we walk in the path of Your judgments. Your name and renown are the desire of our souls.
My soul longs for You in the night; indeed, my spirit seeks You at dawn. For when Your judgments come upon the earth, the people of the world learn righteousness.
Though grace is shown to the wicked man, he does not learn righteousness. In the land of righteousness he acts unjustly and fails to see the majesty of the LORD.
O LORD, Your hand is upraised, but they do not see it. They will see Your zeal for Your people and be put to shame. The fire set for Your enemies will consume them!

units.label: Peace established, other lords renounced
units.note: Your name alone do we confess

verses.text: O LORD, You will establish peace for us. For all that we have accomplished, You have done for us.
O LORD our God, other lords besides You have had dominion, but Your name alone do we confess.
The dead will not live; the departed spirits will not rise. Therefore You have punished and destroyed them; You have wiped out all memory of them.
You have enlarged the nation, O LORD; You have enlarged the nation. You have gained glory for Yourself; You have extended all the borders of the land.

units.label: Labor that gave birth to wind

verses.text: O LORD, they sought You in their distress; when You disciplined them, they poured out a quiet prayer.
As a woman with child about to give birth writhes and cries out in pain, so were we in Your presence, O LORD.
We were with child; we writhed in pain; but we gave birth to wind. We have given no salvation to the earth, nor brought any life into the world.

units.label: Your dead will live, hide until the wrath passes

verses.text: Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust! For your dew is like the dew of the morning, and the earth will bring forth her dead.
Go, my people, enter your rooms and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourselves a little while until the wrath has passed.
For behold, the LORD is coming out of His dwelling to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity. The earth will reveal her bloodshed and will no longer conceal her slain.

shalom.gloss: Peace, doubled for emphasis, meaning something like perfect or complete peace. This wholeness of peace is promised specifically to the one whose mind is stayed on the LORD, tying inward stability directly to the object of one's trust rather than to circumstances.

tsurOlamim.gloss: The Rock of ages, or eternal Rock, a title emphasizing the LORD's unchanging, everlasting reliability as a foundation for trust. Unlike any lofty city that can be humbled and cast into dust, this Rock never falls and never fails, the very security the New Testament identifies with Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4.

basic.context: This chapter is a song meant to be sung by God's people, celebrating a strong city whose true walls are salvation itself rather than stone. It moves through trust in the Rock eternal, patient waiting for God's judgments, honest confession that human effort alone produces nothing lasting, and climaxes in one of the clearest Old Testament promises of bodily resurrection: your dead will live, their bodies will rise.
basic.hermeneutics: This song describes both the settled trust available to God's people now and a resurrection hope that reaches beyond any single historical event. Verse 19's resurrection promise is a genuine, if compressed, seed of what the New Testament makes explicit and central, while verse 14's denial of resurrection to the wicked, by contrast, sharpens the difference between those who trust the LORD and those who set themselves against Him.
basic.originalLanguages: The doubled Hebrew shalom shalom promises a peace that is whole and complete to the one whose mind rests on the LORD, not merely calm circumstances. That trust is anchored in the tsur olamim, the Rock of ages, a title of everlasting, unshakable reliability that Paul later applies to Christ Himself, 1 Corinthians 10:4.
basic.typology: The Rock eternal, unshakable while every lofty human city eventually falls, anticipates Christ, the spiritual Rock that never fails His people. The resurrection promise, your dead will live, their bodies will rise, anticipates and is fulfilled in Christ's own bodily resurrection and the future resurrection of all who trust in Him.
basic.christ: This chapter's Rock eternal, on whom the steadfast mind rests in perfect peace, is fulfilled in Christ, the spiritual Rock that followed Israel, 1 Corinthians 10:4, and the one true foundation who never gives way. Its resurrection promise, your dead will live, their bodies will rise, finds its guarantee and firstfruits in Christ's own resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:20-23, so that all who are united to Him share the same certain hope.
basic.god: God keeps in perfect peace those whose minds are fixed on Him, not because their circumstances are easy but because He Himself is an unshakable Rock. He disciplines His people in distress, honestly measures the emptiness of purely human striving, and yet promises resurrection life to the dead who are His, while inviting His people to hide safely until His righteous wrath against the earth's bloodshed has passed.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 10:4 identifies Christ as the spiritual Rock. 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 grounds the resurrection hope of believers in Christ's own resurrection as firstfruits. Daniel 12:2 offers a similarly early, explicit resurrection promise. Revelation 6:9-11 pictures God's people sheltered briefly while His judgment on the earth's bloodshed plays out, echoing verses 20 to 21 closely.
basic.oneStory: This song moves believers from trusting the LORD as an unshakable Rock, through honest acknowledgment that human effort alone accomplishes nothing lasting, to the astonishing promise that the dead will live again. It anticipates the whole gospel hope secured in Christ, our Rock and our resurrection, in whom trusting hearts are kept in perfect peace both now and forever.

context.literary:
The song of chapter 26 is a liturgy in five movements, and its voice keeps changing. Verses 1 to 6 open with the congregation's declaration, a call at the gates, and an exhortation to trust. Verses 7 to 11 turn to the individual voice of one who waits for God in the night, and then to the unrepentant who see nothing. Verses 12 to 15 return to the first person plural and look back on the tyrant lords. Verses 16 to 18 recall a distress that bore no fruit. Verses 19 to 21 end with an answer from God Himself, and finally the prophet's command to the people.

Word links hold it together. 'Dust' appears twice, and the placement matters: in verse 5 the LORD casts the lofty city 'into the dust,' and in verse 19 He calls those 'who dwell in the dust' to wake and sing. The humbled and the sleepers share the same ground, and only one of them is told to rise. 'Judgments' and 'righteousness' echo through verses 7 to 10, and the verb 'learn' falls on the two sides of a contrast: God's judgments teach the world righteousness in verse 9, but verse 10 says grace alone did not teach the wicked. The word 'dead' appears in verse 14 for those who will not rise and in verse 19 for those who will, which is the structural tension of the whole song.

Birth imagery runs from verse 17 to verse 19. Verses 17 and 18 describe labour that produced only wind, and verse 19 answers with the earth herself bringing forth. The climax, in other words, is an act of delivery that the people could not manage and the earth is made to perform. This is the second of three songs in chapters 25 to 27, and it takes up the strong city of 26:1 against the lofty city of 25:2 and 26:5.
context.historical:
The song is set 'in the land of Judah,' verse 1, and speaks as a community that has lived under foreign rule. The 'other lords' of verse 13 are not named, but the plural suggests a series of overlords, which fits a people who had seen Assyria, then Babylon, then others hold dominion over them. Verse 16 recalls a time of distress and discipline, and verse 18 admits that the people's own labour had not delivered the earth. That sounds like a community writing after the defeat of its hopes, and many readers place the song in or after the exile, though the text does not date itself and an earlier setting under Assyrian pressure remains possible.

Israel's world gave its dead little hope. The dead were the rephaim, weak shades in Sheol, who could not praise God, Psalm 88:10. Isaiah himself had pictured them stirring in Sheol only to mock a fallen king, Isaiah 14:9. Hope in a fuller life beyond death grows slowly through the Old Testament: Job's confidence that he will see God in his flesh, Job 19:25-27, Daniel's awakening of those who sleep in the dust, Daniel 12:2, and Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, whose story is given as a picture of national return but could only be told in the language of resurrection, Ezekiel 37:11-14. Isaiah 26:19 is one of the clearest early statements.

Neighbouring religions told of gods who die and return with the seasons, and the dew and the earth of verse 19 may remind a reader of that world. The song does not borrow the pattern. The LORD alone is confessed in verse 13, and He brings the dead to life by His own word, not by a cycle of nature.

The command in verse 20 echoes the first Passover, when the people were told to stay in their houses until morning while the destroyer passed, Exodus 12:22-23. A people schooled on that story would hear the instruction as an act of trust.
context.canonical:
Within Isaiah the song answers the promise of Isaiah 25:8 that God will swallow up death forever. Chapter 25 states the victory and chapter 26 shows what it means for the dead. Its opening echoes the song of Isaiah 12:2, which also names God 'the LORD GOD' and calls Him salvation. Isaiah 30:15 repeats the pairing of quiet confidence and rescue that verse 3 describes.

Earlier Scripture prepares for each theme. The gates of righteousness in verse 2 recall the entrance liturgy of Psalm 118:19-20 and Psalm 24:3-7, where only the righteous may enter. The dew in verse 19 recalls Hosea 14:5, where God Himself will be like the dew to Israel. The hidden shelter of verse 20 resembles Psalm 27:5 and Zephaniah 2:3, where the humble hope to be sheltered on the day of anger. Verse 21 follows the pattern of Genesis 4:10, where the blood of the slain cries out from the ground.

Later Scripture develops the resurrection hope. Daniel 12:2 and Hosea 6:2 speak in similar words. The New Testament states the promise as fact: Jesus says, 'I am the resurrection and the life,' John 11:25, Paul calls Christ the firstfruits, 1 Corinthians 15:20-23, and Peter calls Jesus 'the living stone,' 1 Peter 2:4, the same figure as the eternal rock of verse 4. The resurrection of the saints at Jesus' death, Matthew 27:52-53, is one place where the Gospel writers seem to see the promise beginning to be kept. The 'little while' of shelter finds its echo in Revelation 6:11, where the martyrs are told to rest a little while longer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author gave a defeated community a song for the long middle of history. It is written for people who have prayed in the night, have been disciplined, have tried hard and have little to show for it. Such people are tempted either to trust their own efforts or to give up. The song says neither will do. Their peace is to be rooted in what God has done and is doing, and their hope is to reach past any national comeback to the dead themselves.

Verse 13 is meant to protect worship. It confesses that other lords have ruled, but 'Your name alone do we confess.' The people are being taught to name God alone as their Lord, even while they live under someone else's government. The contrast with verse 18 is just as pointed. They had 'given birth to wind,' and the author wants them to see honestly that their labour was not saving the earth. The only salvation worth singing about is the one God Himself brings.

The promise of verse 19 is addressed to those whose dead are God's dead. The first hearers had buried people they loved with no sign of rescue, and the song says those graves are not the end. The command of verse 20 then gives them something to do while the promise ripens: shut the door, rest, and trust that God is moving.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter is description, a song of what the people confess and what God will do. There are only three commands, to open the gates in verse 2, to trust the LORD in verse 4, and to go into the rooms in verse 20. Each needs care. The gates are for a righteous nation that remains faithful, and the song does not teach that people earn their entry by effort, since verse 12 says that all they have accomplished God has done for them. Verse 20 is a particular instruction for a particular day of wrath, not a standing order to withdraw from the world. Believers are sent out into it, Matthew 28:19.

Verse 19 should not be read as a technique, as though the dead could be raised by faith or song. It is a promise about what God will do. What the passage invites in the present is the posture of verse 3: a settled mind, resting on God, held in peace. That posture is the response of the believer to every season of waiting, and it does not depend on the removal of danger.

debates.question: Does the resurrection promise in verse 19, your dead will live, their bodies will rise, refer to Israel's national restoration, individual bodily resurrection, or both?

views.label: A metaphor for Israel's national revival
views.case: Some read the dead rising as figurative language for the nation's restoration from exile or defeat, similar to the dry bones vision in Ezekiel 37, a corporate rather than individual resurrection.

views.label: A genuine promise of individual bodily resurrection
views.case: The vivid, physical language, bodies will rise, awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust, and its contrast with verse 14's denial of resurrection to the wicked, suggests a real individual hope, one the New Testament later confirms and fulfills explicitly in Christ.

debates.bearing: The two readings need not be mutually exclusive; national restoration imagery often carries and points toward a genuine individual resurrection hope, and the New Testament's clear teaching on bodily resurrection, grounded in Christ's own rising, confirms that this verse's ultimate meaning includes real, personal, bodily resurrection.

debates.question: How do verse 14, 'The dead will not live,' and verse 19, 'Your dead will live,' fit together?

views.label: Two different groups of dead
views.case: Verse 14 speaks of the former overlords of verse 13, the 'other lords' who ruled Israel, and says they will not rise to rule again. Verse 19 speaks of 'Your dead,' God's own people. The same Hebrew word for the departed, rephaim, stands in both verses, so the contrast is deliberate: the tyrants stay in Sheol, and the people of God are brought out of it.

views.label: A contrast between past and future, or between two readings of death
views.case: Others hold that verse 14 reflects what the community once believed, that the dead are gone for good, and verse 19 overturns it. On this view the song itself moves from the older view to a new hope, so the two verses mark the turning point of the poem rather than two groups.

debates.bearing: On either reading verse 14 is not a general denial of life after death, and the singular promise of verse 19 stands on its own. The New Testament does not leave the wicked in permanent sleep, since Jesus speaks of a resurrection of judgment as well as of life, John 5:29, so the verse is best heard as the end of the tyrants' dominion, with the larger question of their final fate answered later in Scripture.

study.originalLanguages:
The 'steadfast of mind' in verse 3 is two Hebrew words, yetzer samuch. The first, yetzer, is the shape or inclination of the mind, the same word Genesis 6:5 uses for the 'inclination' of the heart that was altogether evil. The second is samuch, supported or leaning, as in Psalm 112:8, where the heart 'is assured.' A mind formed to lean is held up by what it leans on. The trust that follows, 'he trusts in You,' is the verb batach, to rest the weight on something. The song does not describe a character trait that people have by nature. It describes a mind that has been shaped by leaning on God.

The name in verse 4 is Yah YHWH, two names for God together, the short form and the covenant name. The same pairing opens the song of Isaiah 12:2, so the two songs, one at the start of the book's first major section and one here, share an address to God that is intimate and covenantal at once.

The word 'judgments' in verses 8 and 9 is mishpatim. It does not mean only verdicts. It means God's just decisions in history, the ways He sets the world right. To walk in 'the path of Your judgments' is to live in step with His just acts, and to 'learn righteousness' from them is to see what He values when He acts. Verse 10 shows what happens when mercy comes without this learning: the verb for 'grace is shown' is the one from which the word for favour comes, and the wicked take the favour and learn nothing.

In verse 13 the 'other lords' 'had dominion.' The verb is from the root behind the title Baal, master or owner, the root used of a husband in Isaiah 54:5. The phrase reads like a confession that other masters had been taking the place of a rightful husband. The answer, 'Your name alone,' is therefore not a political slogan but a marriage vow.

The most important word in the chapter may be rephaim, used for the 'departed spirits' in verse 14 and the 'dead' in verse 19. In Israel's vocabulary these are the shades of Sheol, who cannot praise God, Psalm 88:10. Verse 14 says the tyrants' shades will not rise. Verse 19 then says the earth will give up her shades, and it uses the same word. The verb in verse 19 is a causative of the root 'to fall,' and the same root appears in verse 18 in the sense of births that did not come. The people could not make the inhabitants of the world 'fall,' that is, be born, and now the earth makes her dead 'fall' into life.

And 'bodies' in verse 19 translates a Hebrew word for a corpse, so the promise concerns real dead bodies, not spirits. The 'dew of the morning' is literally the dew of lights, the dew of dawn, a picture of life coming up out of the dark ground as the sun comes up.

typology.type: The strong city with open gates, the city whose walls are salvation
typology.fulfillment: The song sets a strong city against every lofty human one, with salvation as its walls and ramparts and gates opened to the righteous, verse 2. Psalm 118:19-20 uses the same entry language. In Revelation 21:12-14 the city has a great wall, twelve gates and twelve foundations, and its gates 'will never be shut,' Revelation 21:25. The escalation is that the wall now carries the names of the tribes and the apostles of the Lamb, the whole people of God. The type falls short because Judah's city was a place on a map that could be, and was, laid low.

typology.type: The Rock eternal, from Horeb to Christ
typology.fulfillment: The Rock of verse 4 stands under the song's trust. Paul reads Israel's wilderness history and says the spiritual rock that accompanied them 'was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. Peter calls Jesus 'the living stone,' 1 Peter 2:4, and Jesus Himself describes the wise man's house built on rock that stood when the storm broke, Matthew 7:24-25. The correspondence is a pattern of reliability and identity. The type falls short in that a rock cannot love or answer, whereas the Rock of the New Testament is a person who loves His people.

typology.type: Labour that gave birth to wind, answered by the earth bringing forth
typology.fulfillment: The nation's anguished labour produced no life, verse 18, and then the earth brings forth her dead, verse 19. The New Testament picks up the language of birth pains for the age to come, John 16:21, and calls Christ 'the beginning and firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:18. Where the people could not give life to the world, the One raised from the dead becomes the first of a new birth, Acts 26:23. The correspondence is real but the pattern is not forced. The text does not predict a person here. It supplies the failure that the gospel then answers.

typology.type: Shut the door and hide until the wrath passes
typology.fulfillment: The instruction to enter the rooms and shut the doors recalls the Passover houses, Exodus 12:22-23, where a household sheltered under the blood. Jesus uses nearly the same words for private prayer, 'go into your inner room, shut your door,' Matthew 6:6, and Paul says believers' lives are 'hidden with Christ in God,' Colossians 3:3. This is an echo, not a direct citation. It shows a consistent biblical idea that safety comes from where one stands, not from where one runs. It falls short because the biblical shelter is finally a person, not a room.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by its peace. The mind kept in 'perfect peace' is kept by a God who has set up salvation as walls. The New Testament says that what the song promises is a person: 'He Himself is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14, and Jesus says, 'Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you,' John 14:27. Paul describes a peace that 'will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus,' Philippians 4:7, which is almost the grammar of verse 3 with the guard in the foreground. Justification brings 'peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,' Romans 5:1, the settled standing that makes a steadfast mind possible.

It leads to Christ through the Rock. Paul identifies the rock that followed Israel with Him, 1 Corinthians 10:4. Peter calls Him the living stone, rejected by men and precious to God, 1 Peter 2:4. The song's plea, 'Trust in the LORD forever,' becomes in the New Testament trust in the One in whom the LORD Himself has come.

It leads to Christ most of all through verse 19. The song promises that the dead will live and their bodies rise, and the apostles say this has begun. Christ 'has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. He raised Lazarus and said, 'I am the resurrection and the life,' John 11:25, and in His risen body He told His disciples to touch Him because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, Luke 24:39. That detail fits the physical language of verse 19. Paul, standing before Agrippa, says the prophets foretold that the Christ would be 'the first to rise from the dead,' Acts 26:23. Verse 19 is one of the places where that foretelling can be heard.

It leads to Christ through the shelter. The people are told to hide a little while, until the wrath has passed. Paul says believers' life is 'hidden with Christ in God,' Colossians 3:3, and the fuller picture is that He bore the wrath for them. It is not an allegory of the verse but the New Testament's own use of the same idea.

A word of caution applies. The song itself does not mention a Messiah, and verse 14 and verse 19 should not be forced into predictions of one person. What the song supplies is the hope and the shape of the hope, and the New Testament identifies who makes it good.
study.god:
This song shows a God who forms the mind that trusts Him. The mind is 'steadfast,' but the grammar shows that it is held and shaped, and the peace is something He keeps. The peace is not the absence of trouble. The people who sing this have been through exile and discipline. They know God as the one who keeps them whole in the middle of it.

He is the Rock of ages, and the song pairs that with a God who brings the lofty down. The high city, for all its height, is cast into the dust, and the people who trample it are the poor and oppressed, verse 6. There is no tension in this for the song. The Rock does not lean, and the high things lean on what cannot hold them.

He is a God whose judgments teach. When His acts of justice come upon the earth, the world learns righteousness, verse 9. But He does not force the lesson on the unwilling. Verse 10 shows grace given to the wicked and wasted, and verse 11 shows His hand upraised, unseen. God's patience is real and so is its limit.

He is the God who works all that His people do. 'For all that we have accomplished, You have done for us,' verse 12. This is not an invitation to passivity, since the people walk in the path of His judgments, but it is a refusal of boasting. Our labour is held inside His.

He is jealous for His name alone, verse 13. Other lords had dominion, but the people refuse to treat them as lords. And He is the Lord of life who raises the dead, verse 19, the same one who goes out from His dwelling to deal with the earth's bloodshed, verse 21. The earth that has hidden the slain will give them up. That is a God who remembers every death and does not allow the ground to keep a secret.

For worship, the song gives the time and the manner: longing in the night and seeking at dawn, verse 9. It teaches that worship in the dark is not a lesser kind of worship but the very place where trust is learned.

crossReferences.note: The preceding chapter promises that the LORD will swallow up death forever. Isaiah 26:19 shows what that means for the people already in the ground: the dead live, bodies rise, those who sleep in the dust wake and sing. The two verses are a pair, with the first stating the victory and the second naming who benefits.

An earlier song in the same book begins with God as salvation and strength and uses the same double name for God, the LORD GOD. Isaiah 26 repeats the pattern. Trust, song and salvation belong together, and the book's songs mark each stage of its hope.

God's word to Judah is that in repentance and rest they would be saved, and their strength would lie in quiet confidence, but they were not willing. Isaiah 26:3 describes the person who is willing. The two verses show the same truth from opposite sides: the people who trust are kept, and the people who scheme are not.

The psalmist asks whether departed spirits rise up to praise God, using the same Hebrew word, rephaim, that Isaiah 26:14 and 26:19 use. The psalm voices Israel's early fear that the dead cannot praise. Isaiah's song answers it by saying the dead will wake and sing.

Daniel says that many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life and others to shame. This is the clearest later statement of what Isaiah 26:19 promised, with the same picture of sleepers in the dust and with the added division of verse 14's ending.

God tells Israel their hope has perished, and promises to open their graves and bring them up. The vision is given as a picture of the nation's return, yet it is told in the vocabulary of resurrection. Placed beside Isaiah 26:19, it shows how national restoration and the raising of the dead overlapped in the prophets' language.

Job says his Redeemer lives and that even after his skin is destroyed he will see God in his flesh. Together with Isaiah 26:19, it shows that a hope of embodied life beyond death was already alive in Israel's wisdom and prophecy before the New Testament made it central.

Paul says Christ has been raised as the firstfruits, and that as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. The promise of Isaiah 26:19 is a harvest, and Paul names the firstfruit that guarantees it. He also supplies the order: Christ first, then those who belong to Him at His coming.

Paul says the spiritual rock that accompanied Israel in the wilderness was Christ. This connects the Rock eternal of Isaiah 26:4 to the person of Jesus, so that trust in the LORD as the Rock is, for the Christian, trust in the Son.

At the first Passover Israel was told to stay in the house until morning while the destroyer passed over. Isaiah 26:20 uses the same pattern of hiding behind a closed door until the danger has gone by. The people who sing the song have learned to see the old story as the shape of every coming rescue.

The martyrs under the altar cry out for justice and are told to rest a little while longer. This echoes the little while of Isaiah 26:20 and the earth's disclosure of the slain in 26:21. In both texts the dead wait in God's keeping while He gathers what the earth has hidden.

The voice of Abel's blood cries out from the ground. Isaiah 26:21 says the earth will reveal her bloodshed and no longer conceal her slain. The two verses show that the ground itself witnesses to murder, and that God hears it from the first death onward.

Jesus tells Martha He is the resurrection and the life and that whoever believes in Him will live though he dies. Isaiah's promise of awakening is no longer only a future event but a person standing at a tomb, who will say 'Lazarus, come out' and bear the promise Himself.

study.oneStory:
The song speaks to the oldest problem in the story, death. Genesis 3 pronounced it as a sentence, 'to dust you will return,' and every genealogy afterward ends in a funeral. Israel's early faith lived honestly with that. Sheol was a place of silence. Isaiah 26 is where the answer begins to be spoken aloud: the dust is not the last word, and the one who commanded its return can also command its release.

It also answers the story of human effort. Since Babel, people have tried to build their way to security and to make a name. Verse 18 gives the verdict on all of it. 'We were with child; we writhed in pain; but we gave birth to wind.' The Old Testament does not hide that Israel's own faithfulness could not save the world. What the song offers in place of effort is a different kind of birth, by the earth at God's command.

After Isaiah the hope grows. Daniel names two destinies for the sleepers in the dust. Ezekiel's bones give the hope national shape. Between the Testaments many Jews came to expect a resurrection at the end. Then Jesus rose, and the song became a report. Paul can say that Christ is the firstfruits and that the harvest follows at His coming, 1 Corinthians 15:20-23. The church lives in the little while of verse 20, sheltered and hidden, while the world still reels. Believers walk with a steadfast mind, because the Rock has been shown to hold.

The end of the Bible gathers every thread. The strong city of verse 1 comes down as the new Jerusalem, with its walls and gates and no night, Revelation 21:12-14 and 21:25. The earth gives up her slain. The peace of verse 3 becomes a place where there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. Those who dwelt in the dust wake and sing, and the sleepers of Isaiah 26:19 are the same company as the redeemed who stand before the Lamb and say, 'Surely this is our God.'

sermon.title: Live for Your Greatest Desire: Jesus
sermon.why: Piper preaches on Isaiah 26:8, your name and renown are the desire of our souls, unpacking how God-centered desire and trust in the LORD, the very themes running through this whole song of trust, find their full satisfaction in Jesus.

quiz.q: What does verse 3 promise to the one whose mind is steadfast?

options.text: Perfect peace, because he trusts in the LORD.
options.note: Verse 3 ties this perfect peace directly to trust in the LORD, not to circumstances.

options.text: Immediate wealth and political power.
options.note: Not promised in this verse; the promise is inward peace, not wealth or power.

options.text: Freedom from all future hardship.
options.note: The chapter elsewhere describes ongoing distress and discipline, so this overstates the promise.

options.text: A guaranteed long earthly life.
options.note: Not the specific promise of this verse, which concerns inward peace rooted in trust, not lifespan.

quiz.q: What title for God appears in verse 4, emphasizing His reliability?

options.text: The Rock eternal, or Rock of ages.
options.note: Verse 4 names God the LORD as the Rock eternal, tsur olamim.

options.text: The Shepherd of Israel.
options.note: A true biblical title elsewhere, but not the specific title used in this verse.

options.text: The King of kings.
options.note: A true biblical title, but not the specific phrase used in verse 4, which is Rock eternal.

options.text: The Judge of all the earth.
options.note: Used elsewhere in Scripture, but not the title given in this particular verse.

quiz.q: What honest confession do the people make in verse 18 about their own efforts?

options.text: They writhed in labor pains but gave birth only to wind, accomplishing no lasting salvation.
options.note: Verse 18 states this directly, a stark admission of human effort's futility apart from God.

options.text: Their efforts fully saved the nation without God's help.
options.note: The opposite; the confession is that their own efforts produced nothing lasting.

options.text: They successfully brought new life and salvation to the whole earth.
options.note: The text explicitly denies this outcome; no salvation or life resulted from their labor.

options.text: They gave up trying entirely and did nothing at all.
options.note: The image is of real, painful labor and effort, not passivity, that still produced nothing lasting.

quiz.q: What resurrection promise appears in verse 19?

options.text: Your dead will live; their bodies will rise, and the earth will bring forth her dead.
options.note: Verse 19 states this resurrection hope explicitly and vividly.

options.text: The dead will remain in the ground permanently with no hope of rising.
options.note: This describes verse 14's statement about the wicked, the opposite of verse 19's promise to God's own.

options.text: Only a select few individuals will ever be resurrected.
options.note: The verse speaks broadly of the dead among God's people rising, not a narrowly restricted few.

options.text: Resurrection will occur but only in a purely symbolic, non-bodily sense.
options.note: The language, bodies will rise, dwell in the dust, strongly suggests a genuinely bodily hope, not merely symbolic renewal.

quiz.q: What are God's people told to do in verse 20, right after the resurrection promise?

options.text: Enter their rooms and hide briefly until the LORD's wrath against the earth has passed.
options.note: Verse 20 gives this instruction directly, immediately following the resurrection hope of verse 19.

options.text: Go out and confront the coming wrath directly.
options.note: The opposite instruction is given; they are told to hide, not confront the wrath directly.

options.text: Abandon their homes permanently and flee the land.
options.note: The instruction is to hide briefly, a little while, not to abandon the land permanently.

options.text: Gather publicly to celebrate before the wrath even begins.
options.note: The instruction is specifically to hide and shut their doors, not to gather in public celebration at this point.

questions: The steadfast mind is kept in perfect peace because it trusts in the LORD, the Rock eternal. What is currently competing with God to be the rock you actually trust for your peace?

The people honestly confess that their own labor produced no lasting salvation, only wind. Where have you been striving hard at something that, if you are honest, cannot ultimately save or fulfill you?
Verse 19 gives one of the Bible's clearest Old Testament promises of resurrection. How does the certainty of your own future bodily resurrection in Christ change how you view suffering or loss today?

God's people are told to hide briefly until His wrath has passed, trusting His timing rather than facing it themselves. Where do you need to trust God's protection and timing rather than trying to manage a threatening situation on your own?
The song moves from confessing other lords have ruled over them to declaring, Your name alone do we confess. What competing loyalties or lesser lords might God be calling you to renounce this week?

translationNotes.note: Perfect peace renders a doubled Hebrew word, shalom shalom, an intensifying construction suggesting completeness rather than a partial or occasional peace.
This verse's denial of resurrection applies specifically to oppressive powers or the wicked, contrasted deliberately with the resurrection hope promised to God's own people in verse 19.
Your dew is like the dew of the morning uses a vivid image of refreshment and renewal after death, likening resurrection to dew that revives parched ground.
